templates.pattern: Breaking bonds in the reactants requires [BREAK] kJ/mol. Forming bonds in the products releases [FORM] kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction in kJ/mol.
templates.explanation:
ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy released forming bonds
= [BREAK] − [FORM]
= [RESULT] kJ/mol

This method uses average bond energies and gives approximate enthalpy changes. It is less accurate than using formation enthalpies because bond energies are averages.

templates.pattern: Using a Born-Haber cycle: enthalpy of formation = [DHF] kJ/mol, ionisation energy = [IE] kJ/mol, electron affinity = [EA] kJ/mol, atomisation enthalpies sum = [AT] kJ/mol. Calculate the lattice energy in kJ/mol.
templates.explanation:
Born-Haber cycle:
Lattice energy = ΔHf − IE − EA − ΔH_atomisation
= [DHF] − [IE] − [EA] − [AT]
= [RESULT] kJ/mol

Lattice energy is always negative — energy is released when gaseous ions come together to form an ionic lattice. More negative = stronger ionic bonding.

templates.pattern: The lattice energy of an ionic compound is [LE] kJ/mol. The sum of hydration enthalpies of its ions is [HE] kJ/mol. Calculate the enthalpy of solution in kJ/mol.
templates.explanation:
ΔH_solution = ΔH_hydration + lattice energy
Since lattice energy is endothermic when dissolving:
ΔH_solution = ΔH_hydration − lattice energy
= [HE] − [LE]
= [RESULT] kJ/mol

A small or negative enthalpy of solution means the compound dissolves readily. If too endothermic the compound is poorly soluble.

templates.pattern: An ionic compound has cation charge [Q1] and anion charge [Q2]. The interionic distance is [R] pm. Calculate the relative lattice energy using the formula Q₊ × Q₋ ÷ r.
templates.explanation:
Relative lattice energy ∝ Q₊ × Q₋ ÷ r
= [Q1] × [Q2] ÷ [R]
= [RESULT]

Lattice energy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius. MgO has much greater lattice energy than NaCl because Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have double charges.

templates.pattern: A molecule has [NB] electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and [NA] electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals. Calculate the bond order.
templates.explanation:
Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2
= ([NB] − [NA]) ÷ 2
= [NB-NA] ÷ 2
= [RESULT]

A bond order of 0 means no stable bond exists. Bond order 1 = single bond, 2 = double bond, 3 = triple bond. Higher bond order means shorter stronger bond.

templates.pattern: A bond has a partial charge of [Q] × 10⁻²⁰ C and a bond length of [L] pm. Calculate the dipole moment of the bond in debye. (1 debye = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C·m, 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m)
templates.explanation:
Dipole moment μ = Q × r
= [Q] × 10⁻²⁰ × [L] × 10⁻¹²
= [Q*L] × 10⁻³²
Converting to debye: ÷ 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰
= [RESULT] D

Dipole moment measures bond polarity. A larger partial charge or longer bond length gives a larger dipole moment. Symmetrical molecules can have polar bonds but zero overall dipole moment.

templates.pattern: The C-C bond length in a molecule is [BL] pm. Calculate the covalent radius of carbon in pm.
templates.explanation:
Covalent radius = bond length ÷ 2
= [BL] ÷ 2
= [RESULT] pm

Different C-C bond lengths (154 pm single, 134 pm double, 120 pm triple) give different covalent radii for carbon in different bonding environments.

templates.pattern: An atom in a metallic lattice contributes [VE] valence electrons to the delocalised electron sea. The metal contains [N] × 10²³ atoms per cm³. Calculate the number of delocalised electrons per cm³ in units of 10²³.
templates.explanation:
Delocalised electrons per cm³ = valence electrons per atom × atoms per cm³
= [VE] × [N] × 10²³
= [RESULT] × 10²³

The sea of delocalised electrons explains metallic properties — electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and metallic lustre. More valence electrons generally means stronger metallic bonding.

templates.pattern: A reaction has an enthalpy change of [DH] kJ/mol and occurs at a temperature of [T] K. The entropy change is [DS] J/mol·K. Calculate the Gibbs free energy change in kJ/mol.
templates.explanation:
Gibbs free energy ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
= [DH] − ([T] × [DS] ÷ 1000)
= [DH] − [T*DS/1000]
= [RESULT] kJ/mol

If ΔG is negative the reaction is spontaneous. ΔS must be converted from J to kJ by dividing by 1000 before subtracting from ΔH.

templates.pattern: A reaction involves breaking [N1] moles of bond X (BE = [BE1] kJ/mol) and [N2] moles of bond Y (BE = [BE2] kJ/mol) and forming [N3] moles of bond Z (BE = [BE3] kJ/mol). Calculate the enthalpy change in kJ/mol.
templates.explanation:
ΔH = energy to break bonds − energy to form bonds
= ([N1] × [BE1] + [N2] × [BE2]) − ([N3] × [BE3])
= [N1*BE1+N2*BE2] − [N3*BE3]
= [RESULT] kJ/mol

This multi-bond calculation is the standard method for estimating enthalpy changes using bond energies in A-Level chemistry.
